stem: A 14-year-old boy develops sudden wheeze and chest tightness after running outdoors in cold air. He speaks in full sentences. Heart rate is 104/min, and expiratory wheezes are heard on both sides. He has no heart disease.
oneliner: 14M + wheeze, chest tightness after running in cold air + full sentences + diffuse expiratory wheeze → fastest relief?
ask: Which drug gives the fastest relief of his symptoms?

whyNot.A: **Inhaled corticosteroid**: controller with onset over days, not a rescue drug
whyNot.C: **Antimuscarinic**: weaker and slower bronchodilator, not first-line rescue
whyNot.D: **Long-acting beta-2 agonist**: slow onset, used for maintenance, not rescue

why: **Acute wheeze triggered by exercise** = bronchospasm. A **short-acting selective beta-2 agonist** (albuterol) relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes.

drug.name: Albuterol
drug.how: Gs, cAMP up, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle
drug.use: Acute asthma and COPD relief, exercise-induced bronchospasm

stem: A 38-year-old man from a coastal city is booked on a flight to a Colorado ski resort, where he will sleep at 3,000 m on the first night. On a trip last year he developed a headache, nausea and poor sleep at altitude, all of which cleared when he came down. His blood pressure is normal, he is not confused or unsteady, and he wants a tablet to start before the trip.
oneliner: 38M + sea-level resident going quickly to 3,000 m + headache, nausea, poor sleep at altitude last year + wants a tablet → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to prevent his symptoms?

whyNot.A: A loop diuretic causes volume loss and **contraction alkalosis**, which blunts breathing; his **blood pressure is normal** and nothing needs removing
whyNot.B: A thiazide also causes **metabolic alkalosis** and volume loss; it does not stimulate ventilation
whyNot.C: A potassium-sparing diuretic that causes **no bicarbonate loss**, so it does not **drive ventilation**; his blood pressure is normal
whyNot.D: An osmotic agent for **cerebral edema**; he has **no confusion or unsteadiness**

why: **Rapid ascent with prior headache, nausea and poor sleep** at altitude = acute mountain sickness. **Acetazolamide** blocks carbonic anhydrase, so bicarbonate is lost in urine, causing a **mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates breathing** and speeds acclimatization.

drug.name: Acetazolamide
drug.how: Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so bicarbonate is lost in urine, giving a mild metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation
drug.use: Prevention of acute mountain sickness, glaucoma, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, metabolic alkalosis
drug.watch: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, calcium phosphate stones, sulfonamide allergy cross-reactivity

idea.rule: Acetazolamide causes a metabolic acidosis, and the acidosis drives ventilation.
also: Acute mountain sickness: acetazolamide for prevention, descent and dexamethasone for severe disease
At altitude, hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis; acetazolamide speeds the compensatory bicarbonate loss
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: acetazolamide lowers CSF production
Glaucoma: acetazolamide lowers aqueous humor production

stem: A 36-year-old man with asthma and recurrent nasal polyps developed wheezing and nasal congestion within an hour of taking aspirin for a headache. The same reaction followed ibuprofen last year. His urinary leukotriene E4 is markedly raised between attacks. He asks for a daily oral medicine to reduce further attacks.
oneliner: 36M + asthma + nasal polyps + wheeze within an hour of aspirin and of ibuprofen + high urinary LTE4 + wants daily oral prevention → which drug?
ask: Adding which drug would best reduce his attacks?

whyNot.A: A nonselective beta blocker; it **worsens bronchospasm in asthma**
whyNot.B: A cyclooxygenase inhibitor, not a leukotriene blocker; it does nothing for the **raised leukotriene E4**
whyNot.D: An **inhaled** mast-cell stabilizer, not oral, and it does not block **leukotrienes**
whyNot.E: A weak bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic index; it does not counter the **leukotriene excess**

why: **Asthma, nasal polyps and wheeze after aspirin and ibuprofen** is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. COX-1 blockade pushes arachidonate down the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, so the **leukotriene excess (high urinary LTE4)** is best countered by a **leukotriene modifier such as montelukast**.

drug.name: Montelukast
drug.how: Competitively blocks CysLT1 receptors on airway smooth muscle, countering the leukotriene excess that follows COX-1 blockade
drug.use: Asthma controller, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, allergic rhinitis
drug.watch: Neuropsychiatric events (boxed warning); may unmask eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis when steroids are reduced

idea.rule: In aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, blocking leukotrienes treats the cause of the attacks.
also: Samter triad: asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity
Aspirin desensitization is a further option under specialist care
Leukotrienes C4, D4 and E4 cause bronchoconstriction, mucus and edema
